en: The Basket of Conduct (Cariyāpiṭaka),
Chapter on the Elephant King,
Perfection of Virtue (Sīlapāramī) 1
The Practice of Supporting One’s Mother:
“When I was an elephant in the forest, supporting my mother;”
At that time, there was no one on earth equal to me in virtue.
Seeing me in the forest, the forest-dweller—
He reported this to the king:
"O Great King, there dwells in the forest an elephant worthy of you."
There is no need for a measuring cord,
nor even for a plumb line;
once the trunk is grasped, [the whole elephant is captured].
"Come here yourself!
Having heard those words of his,
the king too was delighted in heart.
He sent for a skilled trainer,
one who was well-trained.
Having gone there, that elephant trainer—
He saw Padumassara pulling up the root and stalk of a lotus for the sake of sustaining his mother.
Having recognized my virtue and character,
he observed my marks; then,
saying “Come, son,” he spoke.
He seized me by my trunk.
Whatever natural strength I possessed, inherent in my body at that time;
Today, I am equal in strength to a thousand Nāgas;
if I were to become angry with them here—
I would be capable of seizing those who have approached me,
even for the sake of human sovereignty.
Moreover, for the sake of guarding my virtue and fulfilling the perfection of virtue,
I do not allow any alteration of mind.
While I was being thrown into the pit,
if they were to strike me there with axes and javelins;
“I would not become angry with them, for fear of breaking my virtue.
Thus ends the first chapter, the Practice of Supporting One’s Mother.
